ego.name: Heinz Nixdorf
ego.summary: Heinz Nixdorf was a German computer pioneer and entrepreneur who built a small electronics laboratory into Nixdorf Computer AG, an international producer of business computer systems. He helped establish a market for compact, decentralized data-processing systems and also invested personally in employee training and sports programs.

connections.relationship_description: Nixdorf’s father worked for the railroad. Periods of unemployment left the family short of money, and he died on the Eastern Front in 1944.
connections.notes: After Walter Nixdorf’s death, Heinz helped support his mother and siblings through agricultural work.

connections.relationship_description: Änne Nixdorf, née Ströhmeier, raised Heinz in a financially strained Paderborn household. She opposed his early effort to leave teacher training for an academic education.
connections.notes: After Walter Nixdorf’s death in 1944, Heinz worked in agriculture to help support her household.

connections.relationship_description: Sprick directed the Remington Rand department where Nixdorf became his assistant. He guaranteed Nixdorf’s first RWE funding and transferred inventions and a patent that supported the early laboratory.
connections.notes: Sprick's technical work and financial guarantee helped make Nixdorf's 1952 laboratory possible.

connections.relationship_description: Wierzoich was Nixdorf’s first employee and an early technical collaborator at the Heinz Nixdorf Laboratory for Impulse Technology. He worked with Nixdorf on the ES computer.
connections.notes: He was a trained radio and television technician.

connections.relationship_description: Nixdorf recruited Müller as a development engineer and gave him scope to pursue an independent computer design. Müller created the Wanderer Logatronic and led work on its successor, the Nixdorf System 820.
connections.notes: Müller left Nixdorf in 1969 to establish his own computer-engineering business.

connections.relationship_description: Ilse Müller returned to Germany with her husband Otto when Nixdorf’s company recruited them in 1964. She helped persuade Nixdorf to approve Otto Müller’s desk-computer design.
connections.notes: The main article identifies her as Otto Müller's wife; the related article identifies her as Ilse Müller.

connections.relationship_description: Luft was a senior sales executive at Nixdorf Computer AG. He became chief executive shortly after Nixdorf’s death in April 1986.
connections.notes: Luft had worked for Nixdorf Computer AG for more than 17 years in executive roles before becoming chief executive.

connections.relationship_description: Nixdorf brought former decathlon world-record holder and Olympic bronze medalist Kurt Bendlin into the company’s sports program. Bendlin led training and sports promotion at Nixdorf Computer AG from 1979.
connections.notes: Nixdorf Computer AG included physical training in its employee-development program.

category_summaries.summary: Nixdorf grew up in a household affected by his father’s intermittent unemployment. After Walter Nixdorf died on the Eastern Front in 1944, Heinz worked in agriculture to help support his mother and siblings in Paderborn.

Nixdorf’s technical circle turned early experience with calculating machines into a computer business. Walter Sprick provided mentorship, a financial guarantee, and technical rights for the first laboratory. Alfred Wierzoich helped build the ES, while Otto Müller’s Logatronic and System 820 gave the company its own small-computer systems.

Nixdorf Computer AG linked employee training with organized sport in Paderborn. Kurt Bendlin directed training and sports support from 1979. Klaus Luft represented the company’s sales leadership and became chief executive after Nixdorf’s death.
